domains.label: Core Survival
domains.description: The foundational priorities for staying alive. Rule of 3 governs everything: air, shelter, water, food. Master these before all else.

articles.title: Rule of 3 — Survival Priorities
articles.body:
Survival decisions must be made in order of urgency. The Rule of 3 defines your timeline.

**The Rule of 3**
3 minutes without air (airway obstruction, drowning, cardiac arrest)
3 hours without shelter in harsh weather (hypothermia, hyperthermia)
3 days without water (severe dehydration, organ failure)
3 weeks without food (starvation, though functional decline begins sooner)

**Immediate Priority Checklist**
1. Stop. Breathe. Assess — panic burns calories and causes errors.
2. Check yourself for injuries — adrenaline masks pain.
3. Survey immediate environment — threats: fire, flood, unstable terrain, predators.
4. Assess weather — is shelter your first need, or water?
5. Signal for rescue if that option exists.

**Survival Psychology**
Most survival deaths occur within 24–72 hours, usually from panic-driven decisions. The will to survive is a genuine physiological force: people with clear purpose survive longer than those who give up. Name your reason to survive. Write it down if you have paper.

Fear is normal. Panic is optional. Fear sharpens senses; panic disables them. When panic rises: stop all movement, sit down, breathe slowly for 60 seconds, then assess rationally.

**Decision-Making Framework**
Identify your Stopwatch (what kills you fastest?), your Resources (what do you have?), your Options (what can you do?), and your Action (do the best option now). Reassess every few hours.

**Leadership in Groups**
Assign roles immediately. Idle people spiral into panic. One person must lead — not necessarily the strongest, but the most rational. Rotate tasks. Keep children and injured members occupied with simple jobs: gathering dry leaves, sorting supplies. Shared purpose is survival glue.

articles.title: Risk Assessment in Survival Situations
articles.body:
Every action in a survival situation carries risk. Rational risk assessment is a learnable skill.

**The STOP Method**
Stop — cease movement, conserve energy
Think — what is the actual situation?
Observe — what are all available resources and hazards?
Plan — choose the action with the best risk/reward ratio

**Resource Inventory**
Before taking any significant action, inventory: water on your person, food on your person, tools and fire-making capability, shelter materials within sight, signaling capability, medical needs, companion condition.

**Risk vs. Benefit**
Moving uses 4× more calories than staying still. Moving can lead further from rescuers. But staying is not always right: if shelter is inadequate for tonight's temperature, moving to better shelter is worth the calorie cost.

Risk formula: probability of harm × severity of harm vs. probability of benefit × magnitude of benefit.

**Common Fatal Errors**
— Abandoning shelter before dawn in cold weather
— Drinking surface water without purification
— Overexerting in heat or cold seeking help
— Eating unknown plants to stave off hunger
— Underestimating distance to rescue
— Not signaling rescuers due to embarrassment

articles.title: Finding Water in the Wild
articles.body:
Water is your most urgent survival need after shelter in cold weather.

**Reading the Landscape**
Follow animal tracks downhill — they always lead to water. Watch birds at dawn and dusk; they fly toward water in straight lines. Listen for running water. Dense green vegetation in dry terrain signals groundwater nearby: willows, cattails, and cottonwoods grow only where roots reach water.

**Terrain Signs**
Valleys and ravines collect water. Rocky outcrops collect dew. Dry riverbeds often have water 1–3 feet below the surface — dig at the outer bend where sediment is deepest.

**Collection Methods**
Solar still: Dig a 1-metre pit, place a container at the bottom, cover with clear plastic, weight the centre with a pebble. Produces 0.5–1 litre per day in full sun.
Dew collection: Tie absorbent cloth around legs before dawn, walk through vegetation, wring into container. Can yield 0.5 litres per hour.
Transpiration bag: Tie a clear bag over leafy branches in full sun. Condensation collects in 4–6 hours.

**Desert Water**
Cacti contain water in pulp — cut, mash, and squeeze; do not eat the pulp (toxic alkaloids). Follow dry washes to natural tanks in rock depressions. Tamarisk trees indicate water within 5 metres below surface.

**Never Drink**
Seawater (accelerates dehydration). Urine (concentrates toxins). Unknown liquids. Blood.

articles.title: Water Purification — All Methods
articles.body:
All found water must be treated before drinking unless from a trusted sealed spring.

**Boiling — The Gold Standard**
Bring water to a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000m altitude). Kills all biological threats: bacteria, viruses, protozoa, Giardia, Cryptosporidium. Does not remove chemical contamination.

**Chemical Treatment**
Unscented household bleach (5–8% sodium hypochlorite): 2 drops per litre for clear water, 4 drops for cloudy. Wait 30 minutes before drinking. Does not kill Cryptosporidium — combine with filtration.

Iodine tablets: 1 tablet per litre, wait 30 minutes. Pregnancy risk — do not use for extended periods.

**Biosand Filtration**
Build a layered filter: fine sand (20cm), coarse sand (20cm), fine gravel (10cm), coarse gravel (10cm). Water passes top to bottom. Biological layer (schmutzdecke) forms on top sand within 2 weeks and provides additional pathogen removal. Filter output still requires boiling or chemical treatment for viruses.

**SODIS (Solar Disinfection)**
Fill clear PET plastic bottles, lay on corrugated metal roof in full sun. 6 hours minimum on sunny days; 2 consecutive days on cloudy days. Effective against bacteria and viruses. Does not kill Cryptosporidium at standard solar levels.

**Distillation**
Boil water, capture steam in a cloth or curved surface, collect condensate. Only method that removes heavy metals, salt, and chemical contamination. Essential for seawater.

**Priority Order**
If you can only do one thing: boil. If you have time: filter first, then boil. If long-term: build a biosand filter, boil all output.

articles.title: Water Infrastructure — Wells & Pumps
articles.body:
Long-term survival requires reliable water infrastructure beyond collection and purification.

**Hand-Dug Wells**
Site selection: dig at the highest point of local water table, away from latrines and animal areas (minimum 30 metres). Dig in the morning when water table is highest. Dig a shaft 1 metre diameter for worker access. Shore walls with stones, wood, or concrete rings to prevent collapse.

Typical well depth varies by geology: 5–15 metres in valleys, 15–30+ metres on elevated ground. Stop when you reach saturated soil that refills faster than you can bail.

**Well Casing and Protection**
Line the upper 3 metres with impermeable material (concrete, clay) to prevent surface water contamination. Build a raised curbing wall at least 30cm above ground. Install a cover. Never use the same bucket for drawing water and other tasks.

**Ram Pump (No Electricity Required)**
A hydraulic ram pump uses the energy of a large volume of falling water to pump a small volume to much greater height. Components: drive pipe (long, feeding water at slope), delivery pipe, waste valve, check valve, air chamber. Once established, runs continuously with no external energy input. Can pump water 10× higher than the source drop.

**Gravity-Fed Systems**
If water source is above your settlement, gravity feed through pipes eliminates all pumping. Calculate head pressure: every 10m of height provides ~1 bar pressure. Use flexible pipe or bamboo sealed with clay for distribution.

articles.title: Emergency Shelter — Immediate Construction
articles.body:
Shelter is your first priority in cold, wet, or extreme heat. Hypothermia can kill in hours; heatstroke in less.

**Debris Hut (Cold Weather)**
The debris hut is the best emergency shelter with no materials — body heat alone can keep you alive in near-freezing temperatures.

Site: choose a spot sheltered from wind, away from dead trees and flood zones. Collect a pole 3–4 metres long. Prop the thick end 1 metre off the ground against a stump. Collect dead dry leaves, grass, ferns, bracken — enough to fill a minivan. Pile material both sides of the pole, 1 metre deep. Plug the entrance. Crawl in, plug behind you. Insulation must be thick enough that you cannot feel the cold ground.

**Lean-To (General Use)**
Lash a ridgepole horizontally between two trees. Lean branches against it at 45° to form a wall. Cover with bark, leaves, or tarp. Orient the opening away from prevailing wind. Add a fire reflector wall opposite to redirect heat into the shelter.

**Underground Shelter**
In extreme cold or heat, underground shelters use earth's stable temperature (~10–15°C year-round at 1m depth). Dig into a hillside for a dugout. Shore the roof with timber or flat stone. Leave a ventilation hole. Works equally well for summer heat.

**Cold Weather Rules**
Keep your head and neck covered — 40% of heat loss is through the head. Insulate from the ground: ground conducts heat away from the body 25× faster than air. Dry is life: wet clothing loses 90% of its insulating value.

**Desert/Heat Shelter**
A dark shelter in direct sun becomes an oven. Build a raised sleeping platform 30–60cm off hot ground. Double-roof the structure with an air gap of 30cm — the gap ventilates and the outer roof intercepts direct radiation. Orient openings to catch prevailing wind.

articles.title: Long-Term Shelter Construction
articles.body:
Permanent shelter requires understanding of materials, structure, and thermal performance.

**Timber Frame**
Post-and-beam construction uses vertical posts and horizontal beams to carry roof loads. Joints are mortise-and-tenon or notch-and-lash. No metal fasteners required — correctly made mortise-and-tenon joints are stronger than the timber itself. Use green (freshly cut) timber for shaping, allow to dry in place. Common mistake: using undersized timbers. Minimum 15cm × 15cm for main posts.

**Stone Masonry**
Dry-stone construction (no mortar) can last centuries. Choose stones that are flat on at least one face. Alternate bond — never let two vertical joints line up. Use a through-stone (spanning the full wall width) every metre. Walls should batter (lean inward) slightly. Maximum stable height for dry-stone without buttressing: ~2 metres.

**Adobe / Mud Brick**
Mix clay soil (50%), sand (35%), and straw or grass (15%). Straw prevents cracking. Form into bricks (standard: 30×15×10cm). Dry in shade 2 weeks, then in sun 2 weeks. Walls 40cm thick provide excellent thermal mass — cool in day, warm at night. Protect from rain with large roof overhangs.

**Passive Heating/Cooling**
South-facing windows (northern hemisphere) maximise winter sun. Thermal mass (stone, adobe, water) absorbs daytime heat and releases at night. A trombe wall — dark thermal mass directly behind glass — passively heats interiors. Cross-ventilation (openings on opposite walls) creates cooling airflow. Stack effect: high openings exhaust hot air, drawing cool air through low openings.

articles.title: Friction Fire — Bow Drill
articles.body:
Friction fire is the most reliable primitive fire method. Mastering it before you need it is essential.

**Equipment**
Fireboard: dry, soft-medium hardwood (willow, cedar, basswood, cottonwood, mullein). Grain runs straight. No resins, no bark on the notch area. Thickness: 1.5–2cm.
Spindle: same wood species as board, or slightly harder. Straight, round, 60cm long, 2cm diameter. Smooth rounded tip (top end), blunt pointed tip (bottom).
Bow: curved branch, 60–70cm. Bowstring: shoelace, paracord, rawhide — any cordage that won't stretch.
Hearth board or socket: hard wood or stone for the spindle top.
Catchboard: bark, leaf, or flat stone to catch the coal.

**Technique**
Cut a shallow depression in the fireboard and drill it open with the spindle. Cut a pie-shaped notch from the edge of the hole to the centre: exactly 1/8 of the circle. Powder accumulates in this notch.

Position: one knee down, foot on the fireboard holding it steady. Bow in dominant hand, spindle in bow string (one loop around spindle), socket in off hand pressed down on spindle top.

Stroke: long, even, full-length bow strokes. Maintain constant downward pressure. Speed must be consistent — not faster, just steadier. A good coal typically takes 15–30 full strokes.

Sign of success: thick white smoke, black powder accumulating in notch. Continue 5 more strokes after smoke begins. Carefully tilt the board to roll the coal onto the catchboard. Transfer to tinder bundle, blow gently.

**Common Failures**
Wet wood is the #1 cause of failure. Smoke but no coal: increase downward pressure. Spindle slipping: check bowstring tension. Coal crumbles when moved: too dry; add a tiny drop of moisture to notch.

articles.title: Fire Lays, Fuel, and Fire Management
articles.body:
Starting fire is only half the skill. Managing fire for specific purposes is the other.

**Fire Lay Types**
Teepee lay: fuel leaned in a cone above the tinder. Burns fast and hot — good for boiling water quickly. Burns down quickly; needs constant feeding.
Log cabin lay: fuel stacked in a square around the tinder, like a log cabin. Burns slowly, produces a stable bed of coals — ideal for cooking and warmth.
Star lay: four long logs pointing into a central fire, pushed in as they burn. Extremely fuel-efficient; useful when wood is scarce.
Trench fire: dig a 20cm trench aligned with prevailing wind. Fire in the trench is wind-sheltered and oxygen-fed from below — most wind-resistant fire lay.

**Fuel Sequence**
Tinder: the finest, driest material — grass, inner bark fibres, down feathers, dry leaves, charred cloth. Must light from a single spark.
Kindling: finger-thickness sticks. Must be bone dry. Graduated sizes from match-stick up to pencil thickness.
Fuel: progressively larger wood. Never add large fuel before small fuel is burning strongly.

**Fire for Specific Purposes**
Cooking: a bed of coals, not flames. Let fire burn down for 45–60 minutes before cooking over it. Flames produce soot and uneven heat.
Water sterilisation: full rolling boil required — large bubbles continuously breaking the surface.
Signaling: add green leaves, plastic, or rubber to produce dark smoke visible from aircraft. In snowy landscapes, use black materials; in jungles, white smoke (add water to fire) is more visible.
Warmth: fire + reflector wall behind you doubles warmth. Sleep 1–1.5 metres from fire — closer means burning sparks, further means cold.

**Fire Safety**
Never leave fire unattended. Establish a clear perimeter. In dry conditions, spark arrest is critical. Extinguish completely: pour water, stir, pour again — ashes can remain hot for hours.

articles.title: Solar and Spark Ignition Methods
articles.body:
Alternative ignition methods work when friction fire is impractical due to moisture or physical limitation.

**Magnifying Lens**
A convex lens — magnifying glass, binocular lens, bottle bottom filled with water and tied off, a clear plastic bag of water — focuses sunlight into a small point capable of igniting tinder. Requires bright direct sunlight. Focus the smallest, brightest dot on the darkest, driest tinder. Hold steady for 15–30 seconds. Works: eyeglasses (convex lenses only), camera lenses, telescopes, broken glass bowls, ice lens ground into convex shape.

**Flint and Steel**
Requires flint (or quartzite, chert, jasper, obsidian) and high-carbon steel. Strike flint against steel at 45°, directing sparks onto char cloth or amadou tinder. Char cloth: cotton fabric pre-charred in a tin to create an excellent spark catcher. Much easier than friction fire; flint lasts thousands of strikes.

**Battery Spark**
Touch wire from both terminals of a 9V battery (or two AA batteries in series) to steel wool. Instant ignition. Even partially depleted batteries work. Works in rain if the steel wool is sheltered.

**Fire Starting in Rain**
Split wet logs to access dry interior. Shave off thin curls of dry inner wood for tinder. Look for dead branches still attached to trees (they drain rather than absorb rain). Carry dry tinder in a sealed container at all times. Build fire on a platform of thick logs to insulate from wet ground.

articles.title: Universal Edibility Test
articles.body:
Never eat an unknown plant without performing the Universal Edibility Test. A single misidentification can be fatal.

**The Test — 8 Hours per Plant Part**
Test only one part of a plant at a time (leaves, berries, roots separately). Separate each stage by 8 hours.

1. Smell: crush a small piece. If it smells strongly of almonds (cyanide), rotten meat, or caustic chemicals — discard.
2. Skin contact: rub the juice on the inside of your wrist. Wait 15 minutes for burning, rash, or hives.
3. Lip contact: place a small piece on your lips for 3 minutes. Watch for tingling, burning, numbness.
4. Mouth contact: chew a small piece without swallowing. Hold in mouth 15 minutes. Spit out. Same signs.
5. Swallow small amount (thumbnail size). Wait 8 hours. Watch for nausea, cramping, dizziness.
6. Eat a small portion (50g). Wait 8 hours.

If no reaction at any stage: the plant part is likely safe.

**Automatic Discard Rules**
— Milky or discoloured sap
— Spines, fine hairs, or thorns
— Bitter or soapy taste
— Umbrella-shaped flower clusters (carrot family — contains hemlock)
— Beans, bulbs, or seeds inside pods (many toxic)
— Plants in areas near industrial sites or mining

**High-Value Wild Edibles**
Dandelion (all parts), cattail (young shoots, pollen, rhizomes), nettles (boiled to neutralise sting), plantain (leaves, seeds), purslane (leaves, mucilaginous), wood sorrel (small amounts, very high oxalic acid), pine inner bark (cambium layer — calories in emergency).

articles.title: Trapping and Hunting
articles.body:
Hunting and trapping require skill and patience but provide calorie-dense food.

**Snare Construction**
A simple wire loop snare catches small mammals. Loop diameter: fist-size for rabbits, thumb-and-finger circle for squirrels. Support loop at animal's chin height — use a forked twig to hold it at the right height on the trail. Place on runs — compacted trails through grass visible around burrow entrances and between feeding areas. Check every 4 hours; dead animals decompose quickly. Check local laws (irrelevant in true survival situations but important otherwise).

**Deadfall Trap**
The Paiute deadfall uses a toggle-and-cord mechanism to drop a heavy flat stone onto prey. Bait the trigger with food. A correctly set deadfall is hair-trigger sensitive — small animals trigger it easily. Requires a large flat rock (2–5kg for rabbits), trigger sticks, and cordage.

**Hunting Without Weapons**
Use throwing sticks for small birds and rabbits — practice, but effective at close range. A rabbit stick: a curved stick 60cm long, 4–5cm diameter, weighted end. Thrown low and horizontal, it sweeps a large arc. Construct a simple bow and arrows with fletching — this takes a day to construct properly and many hours of practice.

**Fish**
Spear fishing at night with a torch — fish are attracted to light and stunned by it. Build a weir: a V-shaped rock or stick barrier across a stream, with a basket at the narrow end. Set overnight. Gorge hooks (straight sharpened stick tied in middle) are simpler than hook-and-line and don't require rod or reel.

**Insect Protein**
Insects are the most calorie-efficient protein source. Grasshoppers, crickets, mealworms, ants: remove wings and legs, cook (kills parasites). Avoid brightly coloured insects (warning colouration = toxic). 100g crickets = 210 calories, 20g protein.

articles.title: Food Preservation Without Refrigeration
articles.body:
Preserving food prevents waste and builds reserves for lean periods.

**Drying / Dehydration**
The oldest and most reliable preservation method. Slice meat or fish thin (5mm). Salt lightly if available (draws out moisture, inhibits bacteria). Hang in full sun and wind, or over a slow fire. Jerky is ready when it bends without breaking but doesn't feel wet. Dried fruits: slice, remove pits, dry in sun on flat rocks 3–5 days. Test: should be leathery, not sticky.

**Salt Curing**
Salt draws moisture out of cells and creates an environment hostile to bacteria. Pack meat in dry salt (table salt, sea salt, or rock salt — all work). Ratio: 30g salt per 500g meat. Bury in salt in a sealed container. For dry salt cure: leave 1 day per 1cm thickness. Rinse before cooking.

**Smoking**
Hot smoking (70°C+) cooks and preserves simultaneously — good for 2–3 days. Cold smoking (below 30°C) is primarily for flavour and mild preservation — combine with salt cure. Use hardwood sawdust or chips; avoid pine, which deposits toxic tar. Set up a smoker: fire in a pit, duct through soil to a smoking chamber above. The earth cools the smoke.

**Fermentation**
Salt fermentation (lacto-fermentation): pack vegetables in brine (1–2 tbsp salt per cup water). Submerge completely, seal loosely to allow CO2 to escape. Ready in 3–7 days. Produces beneficial acids that preserve food for months without refrigeration. Works for cabbage (sauerkraut), root vegetables, green beans.

**Root Cellaring**
Root vegetables (carrots, turnips, parsnips, potatoes) store for months at 0–5°C and high humidity. Dig a pit 1m deep (below frost line). Layer vegetables in sand or dry leaves. Insulate pit with straw. Stable through winter.

articles.title: Navigation Without Technology
articles.body:
Never rely solely on GPS or phones. Technology fails; fundamental navigation never does.

**Sun Navigation**
The sun rises in the east, sets in the west. At solar noon (highest point in sky), the sun is due south in the northern hemisphere, due north in the southern hemisphere.

Shadow stick method: push a straight stick vertically into the ground. Mark the tip of its shadow. Wait 15–20 minutes. Mark the second shadow tip. Draw a line between the two marks: this is an accurate East-West line. The first mark is west, the second is east. Draw a perpendicular line for north-south.

**Star Navigation**
Northern hemisphere: Polaris (North Star) is within 1° of true north. Find the Big Dipper (Ursa Major). The two stars forming the outer edge of the cup point directly at Polaris. Polaris is not the brightest star — it's the end of the little Dipper's handle.

Southern hemisphere: no pole star. The Southern Cross (Crux) points south. Extend the long axis of the cross 4.5 times — that point is due south. Confirm by finding the "dark cloud" (Coal Sack Nebula) at the base.

**Map Reading**
Orient the map by aligning its north arrow with actual north (using compass or sun). Identify your current location by cross-referencing visible landmarks (hills, rivers, roads) with map symbols. Choose a destination. Plan a route following terrain features, not straight lines.

Contour lines: close together = steep slope. Far apart = gentle slope. Circles = hilltop or depression (read annotation). V-shapes pointing upstream = valleys. V-shapes pointing downstream = ridges.

**Natural Signs**
Tree growth: trees lean away from prevailing wind, which is usually identifiable from terrain. In northern hemisphere, moss tends to grow more densely on the north (shaded) side of rocks and trees — unreliable but useful as a confirmation. Snow melts first on south-facing slopes in northern hemisphere.

articles.title: Emergency Signaling
articles.body:
Signaling rescuers is often more effective than self-rescue. Understand what works.

**Universal Distress Signal**
Three of anything: three fires in a triangle, three whistle blasts, three shots, three mirror flashes. International recognition. Repeat every 2 minutes. The rule of three is hardwired into search-and-rescue practice worldwide.

**Mirror / Heliograph**
A mirror or any reflective surface can signal aircraft over 50km away. Aim: hold mirror near face. Look through the sighting hole (or create a v-sight with two fingers). Angle mirror to reflect sunlight in the direction of the target. A moving glint is unmistakable from aircraft. Works with watch faces, CD, aluminium foil pressed smooth, signal mirror.

**Signal Fires**
Fires must produce visible smoke. In forests: white smoke (add water to fire) contrasts with dark background. In snow/desert: black smoke (add rubber, plastic, petroleum products, green vegetation) contrasts with light background. Three fires in a triangle, 30m apart, is the international distress signal.

**Ground Signals**
Large ground-to-air symbols visible from aircraft: X = need medical help. Arrow = travelling in this direction. V = need help. Three Vs = need assistance. Minimum size: 10m per symbol. Use contrasting colours: rocks on snow, disturbed soil on grassland, bright materials.

**Whistle**
Three short blasts: help needed. One long blast: all clear. A plastic whistle produces sound at 100–110dB, audible over 1km in calm conditions. It requires far less energy than shouting.

domains.label: Emergency Medicine
domains.description: Life-saving procedures for situations where professional medical care is unavailable. These instructions exist because death is the alternative.

articles.title: Bleeding Control — Hemorrhage Management
articles.body:
Uncontrolled bleeding is the most preventable cause of death in trauma. Act immediately.

**The C-ABCDE Protocol**
C — Catastrophic haemorrhage control FIRST
A — Airway
B — Breathing
C — Circulation
D — Disability (neurological)
E — Exposure (full body examination)

**Direct Pressure**
Pack the wound with the cleanest material available. Apply pressure with the palm of your hand. Do not lift the dressing to check — you disrupt clotting. If blood soaks through, add more material on top. Maintain pressure for a minimum of 10 minutes by the clock.

**Tourniquet**
Apply for extremity wounds where direct pressure fails or you cannot maintain it. Apply 5–7cm above the wound. Tighten until bleeding stops. Note the time in marker pen on the patient's skin — written on the forehead or limb. Tourniquet time: remove within 2 hours if possible; beyond 6 hours risks irreversible tissue damage. A properly applied tourniquet is painful — this is expected.

Improvised tourniquet: a strip of material 4–5cm wide. Narrower materials (rope, wire) cause tissue damage without fully occluding the vessel.

**Wound Packing**
For junctional wounds (groin, armpit, neck) where tourniquets cannot go, pack the wound cavity firmly with cloth. Push material into the wound with a finger until it is fully packed. Maintain firm pressure. This is the correct technique — superficial pressure alone is insufficient.

**Shock Recognition**
Pale, cold, clammy skin. Rapid, weak pulse. Rapid, shallow breathing. Confusion or altered consciousness. Lay patient flat, elevate legs 30cm (not if spinal injury suspected). Keep warm. Do not give water to unconscious patients.

articles.title: Airway Management
articles.body:
Airway obstruction kills in minutes. These techniques require no equipment.

**Head-Tilt Chin-Lift**
For unconscious patient with no suspected spinal injury: place one hand on forehead, two fingers under the chin. Tilt head back, lift chin forward. This moves the tongue away from the airway.

**Jaw Thrust**
For patients with suspected spinal injury: crouch behind the head. Place fingers behind the angles of the jaw (the bony corners). Push the jaw forward without tilting the head.

**Recovery Position**
An unconscious breathing patient must be placed in the recovery position to prevent aspiration of vomit. Roll onto their side. Bend the top knee to stabilise. Tilt head slightly back to maintain airway. Check breathing every 5 minutes.

**Choking — Adult**
Ask "Are you choking?" A patient who can speak has a partial obstruction — encourage coughing. A patient who cannot speak or breathe has a complete obstruction.
5 back blows: heel of hand between shoulder blades, forceful.
5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind, arms under theirs, hands above navel below sternum. Sharply upward and inward.
Alternate until cleared or patient loses consciousness.

**CPR**
30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths (if trained). Rate: 100–120 per minute. Depth: 5–6cm. Allow full chest recoil. Compressions-only CPR is effective if unwilling/unable to do breaths. Continue until the patient recovers, AED arrives, or you are physically unable to continue.

**Chest Injury**
Sucking chest wound: seal with anything occlusive on 3 sides (flutter valve effect). Tension pneumothorax: patient in rapid decline after sealing chest wound — unseal one edge to release trapped air.

articles.title: Head, Spine, and Burns
articles.body:
These injuries require careful management to prevent secondary damage.

**Head Injury**
Monitor for 24 hours after any blow to the head. Danger signs: loss of consciousness, confusion, unequal pupils, repeated vomiting, severe headache, seizures. Deteriorating consciousness means the patient needs surgery — transport immediately if possible.

Never give aspirin or ibuprofen (worsen bleeding). Paracetamol is acceptable for pain. Keep head and shoulders slightly elevated (15–30°).

**Spinal Injury**
Suspect spinal injury after any high-energy mechanism: fall from height, motor vehicle crash, diving, direct blow to spine.
Signs: neck or back pain, tingling or weakness in extremities, inability to move legs or arms.
Do not move unless danger is immediate and movement is the only way to prevent death. If moving is necessary: keep the spine in a straight line at all times. Log roll technique: minimum 3 people, one controlling the head. Improvise a collar from rolled clothing.

**Burns**
Cool the burn with cool (not cold) water for 20 minutes. Remove jewellery and loose clothing around burn — not clothing stuck to wound. Do NOT: pop blisters, apply butter, toothpaste, or oil, remove stuck clothing.

Burn severity:
First degree (red, dry, painful): treat with cool water, no dressing needed.
Second degree (blisters, very painful): cover with clean, non-fluffy dressing. Do not burst blisters.
Third degree (white, brown, or black, often painless): cover and seek urgent care. Fluid loss and infection are the main threats.

Rule of nines (adult): head = 9%, each arm = 9%, chest = 9%, abdomen = 9%, each thigh = 9%, each lower leg = 9%, back = 18%, genitals = 1%. Burns >15% of body surface area require IV fluid resuscitation.

articles.title: Wound Closure and Suturing
articles.body:
⚠ Field surgery carries major infection risk. Only proceed if professional help is unavailable.

**When to Close a Wound**
Close: within 6 hours of injury, clean wound, no signs of infection.
Do NOT close: wounds older than 8 hours, animal bites, puncture wounds, contaminated wounds, signs of infection (redness spreading, pus, warmth, smell). Let these heal by secondary intention (open, packed, dressed).

**Wound Cleaning — The Most Important Step**
Irrigate under pressure: fill a syringe or plastic bag with a pinhole and squeeze. Clean water is adequate. Pressure dislodges bacteria that antiseptics cannot. Irrigate until no visible debris remains. This step matters more than suturing.

**Suturing**
Sterilise needle and thread (or improvise with fishing line): boil for 10 minutes or hold in flame until red, allow to cool. Use a curved needle if available.

Simple interrupted stitch: insert needle 0.5cm from wound edge, exit 0.5cm on the other side, at equal depth. Tie with square knot (right over left, then left over right). Cut tails to 3–4mm. Place stitches 0.5–1cm apart. Approximate, don't overtighten — swelling will occur.

**Improvised Wound Closure**
Butterfly strips: cut strips of tape or clean cloth 1cm wide. Pinch wound edges together. Apply strips perpendicular to the wound. Add horizontal anchor strips above and below.

**Infection Signs — Remove Sutures Immediately If Present**
Increased pain (after 24h pain should decrease, not increase). Redness spreading beyond wound edges. Warmth. Pus. Red streaks radiating from wound (lymphangitis — sepsis is developing). Fever.

articles.title: Drainage, Abscesses, and Field Amputations
articles.body:
⚠ These are last-resort procedures. Only perform if death is the alternative.

**Abscess Drainage**
An abscess is a pocket of pus. It will not heal without drainage.
Signs: firm painful lump that becomes fluctuant (soft, fluid-filled). Surrounding warmth and redness.
Procedure: clean the skin. Use the sharpest available blade. Make a single incision at the most fluctuant point. Do not make a cross incision — a single cut is sufficient. Allow pus to drain completely. Pack loosely with clean cloth to keep it open and draining. Change daily. Do not suture an abscess closed.

**Wound Debridement**
Dead tissue must be removed or infection will overwhelm the body. Use scissors or scalpel. Remove all grey, brown, or black tissue — healthy tissue is red or pink and bleeds when cut. Dead tissue does not bleed. Irrigate thoroughly after debridement. Pack open, dress, repeat daily.

**Improvised Sterilisation**
Boiling (10 minutes) kills bacteria and most viruses. Flame (hold until red, cool before use). Alcohol (70% isopropyl or ethanol) — 30-minute soak. Direct sunlight UV kills surface bacteria on clean surfaces in 4–6 hours (not reliable alone).

**Field Amputation — Absolute Last Resort**
Only performed when: a limb is irreversibly crushed with no circulation, a tourniquet has been applied beyond 8 hours with no help arriving, gangrene is spreading proximally and death is hours away.
This procedure requires: sharp clean blade, tourniquet applied before starting, general or local anaesthetic if any available, sutures and packing. Infection rate is near 100% without antibiotics. Survival is possible if the patient is otherwise healthy and you can pack and manage the wound.

articles.title: Wound Infection Recognition and Treatment
articles.body:
Infection is the primary killer after initial trauma in austere environments.

**Infection Stages**
Local infection: redness, warmth, swelling, pain, pus at wound site. Treat with drainage, irrigation, dressing.

Spreading infection (cellulitis): redness spreading beyond wound, red streaks up limb (lymphangitis). Patient may have fever. Requires antibiotics if available.

Systemic infection (sepsis): fever >38.5°C or hypothermia, rapid heart rate (>100), confusion, rapid breathing. Life-threatening. Requires aggressive treatment.

**Natural Antimicrobials**
Honey: raw, unprocessed honey has proven antimicrobial properties. Apply directly to infected wounds. Manuka honey most effective but any raw honey works.
Garlic: allicin in fresh crushed garlic has broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity. Apply topically or consume raw.
Turmeric + black pepper: curcumin is anti-inflammatory and has antimicrobial properties.
Maggot therapy: blowfly maggots applied to wounds eat only dead tissue and excrete antimicrobial compounds. Counterintuitive but clinically validated.

**Antibiotic Use**
If antibiotics are available: amoxicillin (wounds, respiratory), metronidazole (anaerobic/abdominal infections), doxycycline (broad-spectrum), ciprofloxacin (urinary, gut). Complete the full course. Never share.

articles.title: Disease Treatment — Fever, Diarrhoea, Respiratory
articles.body:
Infectious diseases become epidemic without infrastructure.

**Fever Management**
Fever is a defensive response — do not suppress unless above 39°C or causing seizures.
Cool with wet cloths to forehead, armpits, groin. Increase fluid intake dramatically. Paracetamol (acetaminophen): adult 500–1000mg every 4–6 hours. Ibuprofen alternated with paracetamol can sustain effect. Keep patient cool but not shivering — shivering raises core temperature.

Malaria signs: cyclical fever every 48–72 hours, chills, sweats, headache, muscle ache. If in malaria region, treat as malaria until proven otherwise.

**Diarrhoea and Dehydration**
Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS): 1 litre clean water, 6 teaspoons sugar, 0.5 teaspoon salt. Sip continuously — do not gulp. For children: 50–100ml after every loose stool.

Dehydration signs: dark urine, dry mouth, headache, dizziness on standing. Severe: rapid weak pulse, confusion, inability to urinate.

Rice water, coconut water, or dilute fruit juice are acceptable alternatives to formal ORS.

**Respiratory Infections**
Pneumonia: fever, cough with coloured sputum, chest pain, rapid breathing. Sit patient upright. Maintain hydration. Amoxicillin if available. Recovery position if unconscious.

**Parasite Infections**
Giardia (foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating): avoid tap water, treat with metronidazole.
Worms (intestinal): maintain clean food handling, cook all meat thoroughly. Pumpkin seeds have antiparasitic activity — consume 50g raw seeds on empty stomach.

articles.title: Emergency Childbirth
articles.body:
⚠ Emergency procedure — seek medical assistance if at all possible.

**Preparation**
Clean hands thoroughly — this is the most important infection prevention step. Prepare clean towels or cloth. Boil scissors or clean blade for cord cutting. Prepare cord ties (two clean strings or strips of cloth).

**Normal Labour Signs**
First stage: contractions every 5 minutes lasting 60 seconds, lasting hours (average 12h first baby, 6h subsequent).
Second stage: urge to push, baby's head visible at opening.
Third stage: placenta delivery, 5–30 minutes after birth.

**Delivery**
Support the baby's head as it emerges — do not pull. Gentle counter-pressure with the palm prevents perineal tearing. If the umbilical cord is around the neck, slip it over the baby's head gently, or clamp and cut before delivery continues.

After the head: the baby rotates naturally. Support the head, allow the body to follow without pulling. The baby will come in one or two more pushes.

**Immediate Newborn Care**
Dry immediately and vigorously — this stimulates breathing. Keep warm: wrap in dry cloth, skin-to-skin with mother. Suction mouth then nose if mucus present. Normal for baby to be blue at delivery — should pink up within 60 seconds of breathing.

**Cord Care**
Clamp (or tie tightly in two places) 5cm and 10cm from baby's abdomen. Cut between. Keep stump dry and clean. Do NOT apply anything to the stump except clean dressing.

**Postpartum Haemorrhage**
Most common cause of maternal death. Causes: uterus not contracting, retained placenta, lacerations. Management: fundal massage (rub the uterus through the abdomen firmly and repeatedly — stimulates contraction), breastfeeding (releases oxytocin), ensure placenta is complete.

articles.title: Infant Care and Child Illness
articles.body:
Children and infants have different physiology and require specific management.

**Breastfeeding**
Breast milk is complete infant nutrition for 6 months and remains important to 2 years. It contains antibodies specific to the current disease environment. Colostrum (first milk, yellow) is especially high in antibodies — do not discard it.

If breastfeeding is impossible: goat's milk or cow's milk diluted 1:1 with water is a short-term alternative. Add a small amount of sugar. Not ideal but better than nothing.

**Dehydration in Children**
Children dehydrate faster than adults. Danger signs: no tears when crying, sunken eyes, sunken fontanelle (soft spot on top of head in infants), dry mouth, no urination for 6+ hours, lethargy. ORS is the treatment — persistence and small sips every few minutes.

**Fever in Children**
Above 38°C: use paracetamol syrup (check dose by weight — 15mg/kg). Strip down to minimal clothing. Lukewarm sponge bath. Encourage fluids. Danger signs warranting emergency action: seizure, stiff neck, persistent rash, extreme lethargy.

**Malnutrition**
Signs: failure to grow, hair loss or colour change to red/brown, oedema (swelling) of face and feet (kwashiorkor), extreme wasting. Treatment: frequent small meals of calorie-dense food. Groundnut paste, eggs, animal protein, legumes. F-100 therapeutic food formula: dried skim milk, oil, sugar, mineral mix.

articles.title: Symptom-Based Field Diagnosis
articles.body:
Without lab equipment, diagnosis is based on careful history and examination.

**History Taking**
SOCRATES for pain: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associated symptoms, Timing, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity (0–10).

Key questions: How long? Getting better or worse? Fever? Similar in contacts (suggests infection)? Recent travel? Recent trauma?

**Physical Examination**
Pulse: feel at wrist (radial) or neck (carotid). Normal: 60–100 adult, 100–140 infant. Rhythm: regular or irregular?
Respiration: count breaths for 60 seconds. Normal: 12–20 adult. Laboured breathing? Using neck/shoulder muscles?
Temperature (improvised): feel forehead and compare to examiner's own — fever = noticeably hotter than normal.
Skin: colour (pale = anaemia/shock, yellow = jaundice, blue = oxygen lack), moisture (sweaty = fever/shock), texture.

**Abdomen Assessment**
Gently press in four quadrants. Guarding (muscle tensing) indicates inflammation below. Rebound tenderness (pain worse on release than on press) indicates peritonitis — surgical emergency. Rigid abdomen is an emergency.

**Neurological Check (AVPU)**
A — Alert (normal)
V — responds to Voice
P — responds to Pain only
U — Unresponsive
Any deterioration on AVPU requires urgent action. Check pupils: equal and reactive to light is normal. Unequal pupils after head injury = intracranial pressure rising.

domains.label: Food Production
domains.description: Feeding communities long-term. Soil science, crop cultivation, permaculture, aquaculture, and food security.

articles.title: Soil Assessment and Rapid Improvement
articles.body:
Healthy soil is the foundation of all food production. Without it, crops fail.

**Soil Types**
Sandy soil: drains fast, warms quickly, poor nutrients. Add compost and clay. Squeeze test: doesn't hold shape.
Clay soil: holds nutrients, waterlogged, compacts. Add compost, sand, biochar. Squeeze test: holds shape easily.
Loam: ideal mix. Holds moisture but drains excess. Squeeze test: holds shape but crumbles when poked.
Silt: medium drainage, can compact. Needs organic matter.

**Soil Structure Test**
Jar test: fill a jar 1/3 soil, top with water, shake vigorously. Let settle for 48 hours. Sand settles first (bottom), then silt (middle), then clay (top layer). Organic matter floats.

**Nutrient Cycles**
Nitrogen (N): leafy growth, green colour. Depleted by heavy cropping. Replaced by legume cover crops, compost, animal manure. Signs of deficiency: yellowing of older leaves starting at tip.
Phosphorus (P): root development, flowering, fruiting. Replaced by bone char, rock phosphate, composted manure. Deficiency: purple or reddish leaves.
Potassium (K): disease resistance, fruit quality, water regulation. Replaced by wood ash, compost, seaweed. Deficiency: brown leaf edges.

**Composting**
Hot compost: alternate layers of brown (carbon) and green (nitrogen) materials in equal volume. Browns: dry leaves, straw, cardboard. Greens: kitchen scraps, fresh grass, animal manure. Keep moist but not wet. Turn every 3 days. Reaches 55–65°C (kills weed seeds and pathogens). Ready in 3–4 weeks. Finished compost smells earthy, not rotten.

**Biochar**
Charred organic matter (not ash). Microporous structure holds water and nutrients and provides habitat for soil microbes. Apply at 10–20% by volume to sandy or degraded soil. Do not apply fresh — it will absorb nutrients from soil. Charge first by mixing with compost or urine for 2 weeks.

articles.title: Composting, Biofertilizers, and Soil Regeneration
articles.body:
Advanced soil restoration techniques for long-term food security.

**Worm Composting (Vermicomposting)**
Red wigglers or compost worms process kitchen scraps into premium compost 5× faster than hot composting. Build a wooden box 60cm × 90cm × 30cm. Add bedding (shredded paper, dry leaves). Add worms. Feed kitchen scraps (no meat, dairy, or citrus in large amounts). Worm castings are the highest quality compost available — high in plant-available nutrients and beneficial microbes.

**Liquid Fertilisers**
Compost tea: steep finished compost in water 24–48h. Apply to roots or spray on leaves. Inoculates soil with microbes.
Weed tea: pack a bucket with comfrey, nettles, or weeds. Top with water. Cover (smells). After 2–4 weeks, strain and dilute 1:10. High in nitrogen and trace minerals.
Human urine: dilute 1:10 with water. Apply to soil (not leaves). Rich in nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Sterile when fresh. Best fertiliser available with zero cost. Apply in morning.

**Biofertilizers**
Rhizobium bacteria: naturally colonise legume roots, fixing atmospheric nitrogen. Inoculate legume seeds with soil from a previously successful legume planting or commercial inoculant. Fixes 100–300kg N/hectare/year — equivalent to expensive synthetic fertiliser.

Mycorrhizal fungi: form symbiotic networks with plant roots, extending their reach dramatically. Don't kill them with fungicides. Build up over years of minimal-tillage farming.

**Soil Regeneration Timeline**
Severely degraded soil: Year 1 — green manure cover crop (buckwheat, phacelia). Year 2 — legume cover crop + compost. Year 3 — first food crops. Year 5 — increasingly productive soil.

articles.title: Staple Crops — Calorie Production
articles.body:
These crops provide the bulk of human calorie needs and must be prioritised in food production.

**Potatoes**
Highest calorie yield per unit of land of any crop. Grow in any temperate climate. Plant in spring, harvest in autumn. Set seed potatoes with at least 2 eyes each, 10cm deep, 30cm apart. Earth up stems as they grow. Harvest when plants die back. Store in cool, dark, frost-free conditions. Avoid green potatoes (solanine toxicity). Yield: 20–40 tonnes/hectare.

**Sweet Potatoes**
Tropical equivalent of potato. Extremely drought tolerant. Plant slips (shoots from old sweet potato). Very fast growing, also provides edible leaves. Yield: 15–30 tonnes/hectare.

**Maize (Corn)**
High calorie yield, versatile. Grows in warm climates. Plant in blocks (not rows) for wind pollination. Needs 60–100 days. Harvest when husk dries. Dry thoroughly before storage. Must be nixtamalised for full nutrition (process with lime or wood ash — releases niacin and amino acids not otherwise bioavailable). Yield: 5–10 tonnes/hectare.

**Wheat and Barley**
The foundation of most civilisations. Plant in autumn (winter wheat) or early spring. Harvest when stalks dry and golden. Thresh by beating, winnow by wind. Store dry or grind into flour. Both malting (beer) and bread. Barley is hardier in cold climates. Yield: 2–5 tonnes/hectare.

**Rice**
Feeds more people than any other crop. Requires warm temperatures and water (paddy rice) or well-watered soil (upland rice). Transplant seedlings from nursery at 30-day age. Harvest when 80% of grains are yellow. Dry thoroughly before storage. Process: remove hull (husking), optionally remove bran (milling).

**Legumes — Nitrogen and Protein**
Beans, lentils, peas, chickpeas: essential complement to cereals. Provide complete protein when combined with grains. Also fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil. Yield: 1–3 tonnes/hectare.

articles.title: Vegetable and Fruit Cultivation
articles.body:
Vegetables provide vitamins and minerals absent from calorie-only diets.

**Priority Vegetables for Nutrition**
Dark leafy greens (kale, spinach, amaranth): iron, calcium, vitamins A, C, K. Hardy, fast-growing. Can be grown in partial shade.
Root vegetables (carrots, turnips, beets, parsnips): store well, provide energy and vitamins. Long season crops.
Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, kohlrabi): cold tolerant, vitamin C. Can be stored for months (cabbage = sauerkraut).
Squash/pumpkin: high yield, stores for months, seeds are edible protein source.
Tomatoes and peppers: high vitamin C, grows in warm climates.

**Succession Planting**
Stagger plantings every 2–3 weeks. One row of lettuce, then another 2 weeks later. Extends harvest season and prevents glut/shortage cycles.

**Companion Planting**
Three Sisters (Native American): maize + beans + squash together. Maize provides climbing structure for beans. Beans fix nitrogen. Squash shades ground, retaining moisture and suppressing weeds. All three grown together outyield monocultures.

**Fruit Trees**
Investment in perennial production. A fruit tree takes 3–7 years to produce but then yields for decades with minimal input. Apples, pears, plums, cherries for temperate climates. Mangoes, papayas, citrus for tropical. Plant in autumn or early spring while dormant. Mulch generously around base.

articles.title: Crop Disease Control and Permaculture
articles.body:
Sustainable crop production requires ecological thinking, not industrial inputs.

**Crop Disease Identification**
Powdery mildew: white powder on leaves. Treat with dilute baking soda spray (1 tbsp/litre) or milk spray (1 part milk, 9 parts water).
Late blight (potatoes, tomatoes): brown, water-soaked patches, rapidly spreading. Remove all affected material immediately. Copper sulphate spray (Bordeaux mixture) as preventative.
Rust: orange-brown pustules on leaves. Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation.
Root rot: wilting despite adequate water. Improve drainage. Remove affected plants.

**Integrated Pest Management**
Companion planting to repel pests: marigolds repel nematodes, basil repels aphids, nasturtium as a trap crop for aphids.
Physical barriers: row covers, copper tape (slugs), sticky bands on tree trunks.
Beneficial insects: ladybirds, lacewings, parasitic wasps eat pests. Attract by planting flowers in field margins.
Neem oil: derived from neem tree seeds. Broad-spectrum insecticide that doesn't harm mammals. Apply when pests first appear.

**Permaculture Principles**
Observe and interact before making major changes. Catch and store energy (water, soil fertility, seeds). Obtain a yield from every element. Apply self-regulation — the system should become self-managing over time. Use edges: the boundary between forest and field is the most productive zone. Value the marginal.

**Food Forest**
Mimic a forest's layered structure with edible plants at each layer: canopy trees (fruit, nut), understory (smaller fruit trees), shrubs (berry, nitrogen-fixing), herbaceous (vegetables, herbs), ground cover (strawberries, herbs), root zone (root vegetables), climbers (grape, kiwi). A mature food forest produces food for decades with minimal maintenance.

articles.title: Fish Farming and Integrated Systems
articles.body:
Aquaculture provides protein and can be integrated with crop production.

**Basic Pond Construction**
Site: flat or gently sloping land with clay-rich soil that holds water. Avoid rock. Build a simple earth embankment (bund). Typical pond: 0.1–0.5 hectares, 1–2m deep. Include an inlet for water entry and a drainage sluice for harvesting and management.

**Fish Species Selection**
Tilapia: most common freshwater aquaculture fish. Fast growing, omnivorous, tolerant of poor water quality. Cannot survive below 12°C.
Carp: tolerant of low oxygen. Grows in cold water. Multiple species: common, grass, silver carp.
Catfish: bottom feeder. Very tolerant of overcrowding.
Trout: requires clean, well-oxygenated water. For cool climates.

**Feeding and Water Management**
Fertilise pond with compost or manure to grow phytoplankton (fish food). Feed with agricultural waste: crop residues, bran, food waste, insects. Natural ponds can produce 500–1000kg/hectare/year without supplemental feed. With feed: 3,000–5,000kg/hectare/year.

**Integrated Rice-Fish Farming**
Stock fish directly in rice paddies. Fish eat insects and weeds, reducing pest pressure. Fish faeces fertilise rice. Rice provides shade, reducing algae. Both yields improve. Stock 500 fish per 0.1 hectare. Choose carp or tilapia.

**Harvesting**
Drain the pond partially to concentrate fish for harvesting. Use nets or baskets. Leave some fish for breeding stock. Restock with fingerlings annually or allow natural breeding.

articles.title: Seed Banks and Genetic Diversity
articles.body:
Seeds are the foundation of food production. Preserving seed is preserving civilisation.

**Why Seed Banks Matter**
Modern agriculture depends on a handful of hybrid varieties. In collapse, hybrid seeds cannot be replanted because their offspring revert to unpredictable forms. Preserve open-pollinated (OP) and heirloom varieties — these breed true.

**Seed Saving by Crop Type**
Tomatoes, peppers, squash: allow fruit to fully ripen on plant. Ferment seed (tomatoes) to remove gel coating. Wash, dry thoroughly on paper towels. Store in labelled paper envelopes, not plastic.
Beans, peas, corn: leave seed pods on plant until completely dry. Thresh, clean, dry further at room temperature (not heat). Test viability: place 10 seeds on damp paper towel in warmth. 8–10 germinating = excellent. Below 5 = discard or plant more densely.
Leafy greens, roots (brassicas): allow plants to bolt (flower) in second year. Collect seeds from dried seed pods. Prevent cross-pollination between varieties by distance (50–500m depending on species).

**Storage Conditions**
Temperature × humidity = seed longevity. Ideal: 0–10°C, <40% relative humidity. Each 5°C reduction doubles storage life. Dry seeds to <8% moisture content before storage. Add silica gel packets. Store in sealed containers in the coolest available location.

**Minimum Viable Seed Bank**
At minimum: 3–5 varieties of high-calorie staples (potato, bean, squash), 3 vitamin crops (dark leafy green, root vegetable, allium), 1 nitrogen fixer (legume), 1 grain if climate allows. At least 50 seeds per variety, ideally 200.

domains.label: Water Infrastructure
domains.description: Long-term water supply, purification, distribution, and sanitation for communities.

articles.title: Groundwater and Terrain Reading
articles.body:
Identifying sustainable water sources is critical before establishing any settlement.

**Identifying Groundwater**
Certain vegetation reliably indicates shallow groundwater: willow, cottonwood, alder, cattail, sedge. These plants require roots near the water table.

Converging valleys concentrate groundwater. The inside of a river meander has the shallowest water table. Rocky outcrops at the base of hills often have springs.

**Divining is Not Reliable**
Water witching (dowsing) has no scientific support. Use geological and botanical indicators instead.

**Spring Development**
A natural spring is the best possible water source. Clear the area around the spring. Dig 0.5m into the hill above to expose the water-bearing layer. Create a collection chamber with flat stones. Build a closed concrete or stone box around it. Install an overflow pipe. Fence animals out — 30m minimum. Chlorinate the chamber annually.

**Groundwater Quality**
Uphill land use determines quality. Farms above your water source mean nitrates. Industry means heavy metals. Septic systems mean bacteria. Test water visually (colour, clarity), by smell, and by boiling before drinking. Boiling removes all biological threats but not chemicals.

articles.title: Waste Management and Latrine Construction
articles.body:
Sanitation failure is the most common cause of disease epidemic after disaster.

**Why Sanitation is Critical**
Cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A, and most diarrhoeal diseases spread via the faecal-oral route: excrement contaminates water or hands, which contaminate food. Simple sanitation breaks this cycle.

**Latrine Construction**
Site selection: minimum 30m from water sources and wells. Downhill from water sources. At least 3m deep if possible to prevent groundwater contamination.

Pit latrine: dig a pit 1m × 1m × 2m minimum. Build a stable superstructure. Install a platform with a squatting hole or toilet seat. Cover hole when not in use (prevents flies). Add ash or dry soil after each use (deodorises and accelerates decomposition). Move latrine when 3/4 full.

Ventilated improved pit (VIP) latrine: add a vertical ventilation pipe extending 50cm above the superstructure. Cover the vent with fly screen. Flies enter through the toilet hole, navigate to the light at the vent, cannot exit through the screen, and die. Reduces odour and fly transmission.

**Handwashing**
Most diseases prevented by this one action. Build a tippy-tap: a plastic bottle on a stick, tilted by foot pedal, delivers water hands-free. Keep soap available at every hand-washing station.

**Sewage Treatment**
For larger groups: build a septic tank (underground sealed chamber, waste decomposes anaerobically), with a soakaway trench 3m long per person. Sludge needs pumping every 3–5 years.

domains.label: Construction & Engineering
domains.description: Building durable structures and infrastructure from available materials. Timber, stone, adobe, structural principles, roads, and bridges.

articles.title: Timber Frame and Stone Construction
articles.body:
Structural knowledge prevents buildings from killing their occupants.

**Structural Principles**
A structure must transfer loads from roof to ground without collapsing. Every load path must be continuous. Triangle is the only inherently rigid shape — all structural bracing uses triangles.

**Timber Frame Construction**
Post-and-beam: vertical posts carry beams which carry rafters which carry roof. All connections transfer load by bearing, not by fasteners.
Wood selection: use straight-grained, knot-free heartwood where possible. Check for cracks along the grain. Avoid sapwood (light-coloured outer layer) for structural members — it decays faster.
Joint types: mortise-and-tenon (most common structural joint), lap joint, scarf joint (extending length). A tenon should be 1/3 the thickness of the timber.
Roof pitch: steep roofs shed rain and snow better. Minimum 4:12 pitch (rise:run) for tiled roof, 2:12 for metal sheeting.

**Stone Masonry**
Select stones for flatness on at least one face. Larger base stones, smaller as you go up. Alternate the direction of stones layer by layer. Fill gaps with small stones and mortar or dry-packed smaller stones. Throughstones (spanning full wall width) every 0.6–0.9m tie both faces together. Walls must have solid foundations on undisturbed ground or bedrock.

**Load Distribution**
An arch distributes load as compression through the arch's curve. Arch and vault construction allows wide spans without timber. Keystone at the arch apex locks the structure. Formwork (temporary timber support) must be built to pour or set the arch, then removed.

articles.title: Adobe, Rammed Earth, and Passive Design
articles.body:
Earth construction is low-cost, local, and thermally excellent when done correctly.

**Adobe (Mud Brick)**
Test your soil: squeeze moist soil into a ball, drop from 1m. Clay-rich soil holds together; sandy soil crumbles. Ideal mix: 25–50% clay, remainder sand and grit. Straw addition (10% by volume) provides tensile strength, prevents cracking.

Making bricks: mix soil with water to stiff paste. Form in wooden moulds (standard: 30×15×10cm). Firm in mould, remove immediately. Dry in shade first (2 weeks), then sun. Bricks must ring when tapped — hollow sound indicates insufficient clay.

Adobe mortar: same mix as bricks, slightly wetter. Lay bricks in staggered bond. Wall thickness: minimum 30cm for structural, 40cm+ for good thermal performance. Protect with large roof overhang (60cm minimum) — rain is adobe's enemy.

**Rammed Earth**
Similar soil mix to adobe. Pack moist earth into a form in 15cm lifts, compact with a rammer until it rings. Produces very dense, hard walls. No bricks needed — monolithic walls. Stronger than adobe but requires formwork.

**Passive Design Principles**
Thermal mass: massive walls (stone, adobe, concrete) absorb heat during the day and release it at night, moderating temperature extremes. Most effective in climates with large day/night temperature swings.
Orientation: main windows face the equator (south in northern hemisphere, north in southern). This maximises winter sun exposure.
Ventilation: stack effect — cool intake at low level, warm exhaust at high level — provides ventilation without fans.
Insulation: different from thermal mass. Insulation resists heat flow; mass stores heat. Cold climates need insulation. Hot climates with mild nights need mass.

articles.title: Earthquake and Storm-Resistant Construction
articles.body:
Building to resist natural forces requires understanding how structures fail.

**Earthquake Principles**
Earthquakes create horizontal forces. Unreinforced masonry (brick, block, stone) fails catastrophically — it has no tensile strength and collapses suddenly. Timber frame and rammed earth perform better.

Reinforcement: add vertical steel rods or bamboo into masonry at corners, openings, and every 1.5m. Connect horizontal bond beams of timber or reinforced concrete at wall top. Connect roof structure to walls — unconnected roofs slide off in earthquakes.

Ring beam: a reinforced concrete or timber beam on top of all walls ties them together. This is the most cost-effective earthquake upgrade for masonry buildings.

**Storm-Resistant Construction**
Roofs fail before walls. Roof failures occur because: the roof is not tied down to the walls, the pitch is too steep (catches wind), the connections between rafters are weak.

Tie-down: use metal straps, large bolts, or thorough timber joinery to connect rafters to wall plates and wall plates to walls. In hurricane zones, provide uplift resistance at every rafter.

Low-pitch hip roofs (sloped on all four sides) perform better in wind than gabled roofs (vertical end walls). Avoid large overhangs in high-wind zones.

**Flood-Resistant Construction**
Elevate floor level 0.5–1m above highest known flood level. Use waterproof materials below potential flood height (concrete, stone, treated timber). Design exit routes above flood level. Install gates or barriers for seasonal flooding.

articles.title: Roads, Drainage, and Bridges
articles.body:
Infrastructure enables trade, communication, and collective action.

**Road Construction**
Even a basic road dramatically increases productivity. Remove vegetation and topsoil. Cut or fill to create a level grade (maximum 10% slope for wheeled vehicles). Crown the road surface (slightly higher in the centre) so water drains to ditches on either side. Compact the surface. Gravel roads: apply 15cm of graded aggregate (varied sizes compact better). Maintain drainage ditches clear of vegetation.

**Drainage Systems**
Water damage destroys roads faster than traffic. Culverts: pipes or stone channels under the road to carry water. Sizing rule: cross-sectional area equals 1 sq cm per 2 sq m of upstream drainage area. Headwalls prevent scour at culvert ends.

**Bridges**
Determine the required span. Simple log bridge (under 5m): two parallel logs of sufficient diameter, decking lashed or nailed perpendicular. Timber trestle bridge: a series of A-frames with longitudinal stringers. All joints loaded in bearing (strongest direction of timber). Foundation: piers or abutments on bedrock or well-compacted fill. Calculate dead load (structure weight) + live load (traffic) + dynamic load (movement and bounce) × safety factor 3.

**Flood Control**
Earthen bunds (levees): compact earth embankments parallel to waterways. Must be higher than 100-year flood level. Slope outer faces at minimum 1:2 (vertical:horizontal). Core of clay for impermeability. Regularly inspect for animal burrows, seepage, and erosion.

domains.label: Energy Production
domains.description: From wood fire to electrical power. Primitive to modern energy systems using available materials.

articles.title: Wood Energy, Charcoal Kilns, and Biomass
articles.body:
Wood is the foundational energy source after civilisational collapse.

**Wood Energy Systems**
Firewood selection: dense hardwoods (oak, ash, beech, hickory) produce more energy per volume than softwoods (pine, spruce). Dry wood burns hotter and cleaner. Freshly cut wood is 50% water by weight — dry for 6–24 months.

Rocket stove: a highly efficient biomass stove. An L-shaped combustion chamber: horizontal fuel feed, vertical chimney. Air enters under the fuel, creating a powerful draught. Uses 75% less wood than an open fire. Build from brick, clay, or stone. Burns sticks, not logs. Produces minimal smoke when burning dry wood.

Mass heater (rocket mass heater): a rocket stove connected to a thermal mass bench or floor. The hot gases travel through a long thermal mass before exiting. The mass stores heat and radiates for 12–24 hours after the fire is extinguished. Extremely efficient for space heating.

**Charcoal Production**
Charcoal stores twice the energy of an equal weight of wood. Burns hotter and cleaner. Required for iron smelting, cooking in enclosed spaces, medical use (activated charcoal).

Retort kiln: stack dry wood in an enclosed metal barrel with a small opening. Heat the barrel from outside. Gases and smoke exit through the opening and can be burned for additional heat. When only clear gas exits, stop heating. Cool completely before opening (risk of spontaneous combustion). Yield: approximately 25% of the dry wood weight.

Pit kiln: dig a pit, fill with wood, start fire, cover with earth when fully burning, leave small airhole, seal completely after 2–3 hours. Yield: 15–20% of dry wood weight.

**Biomass Gasification**
Heat biomass in restricted oxygen, producing combustible gas (syngas: H₂ + CO). This gas can run a modified internal combustion engine. A complete biomass gasifier can convert wood chips or agricultural waste into electricity via a generator. Construction is complex but uses local materials.

articles.title: Waterwheels, Windmills, and Treadmills
articles.body:
Mechanical power from water and wind multiplies human labour enormously.

**Waterwheel Design**
Undershot wheel: wheel sits in the flow, water pushes the bottom. Simple to build. Efficiency 15–30%. Suitable for slow, wide rivers.
Breastshot wheel: water enters at mid-height, combination of impulse and weight. Efficiency 50–60%.
Overshot wheel: water delivered to the top, gravity drives rotation. Most efficient: 70–85%. Requires a sufficient head of water (height difference). Build a millrace (channel) to direct water flow to the top of the wheel.

Sizing: a 3m diameter overshot wheel in a 0.5m³/s flow produces approximately 3–5kW of mechanical power — enough to grind grain, pump water, or power a small forge bellows.

**Windmill Design**
Savonius rotor: two half-cylinders arranged to catch wind in both directions. Very simple to build. Starts in low winds. Efficiency ~15%. Good for pumping water in low-wind areas.

Horizontal axis wind turbine (HAWT): the familiar three-blade design. Efficiency 35–45%. Requires a tower. Blades must track into the wind. A 2m diameter rotor in 6m/s (12mph) average wind produces ~100W continuously — enough for lighting and small electronics.

Blade construction: whittle or steam-bend blades with an airfoil cross-section: rounded leading edge, tapered trailing edge, slightly twisted along the length. Correct pitch: 12–15° at root, 4–5° at tip.

**Human-Powered Machinery**
Treadle loom, treadle lathe, and treadle-powered workshops were widespread before electrification. A human produces 75–100W continuously (cycling), 300W in short bursts. Flywheel stores energy between power strokes. For heavy machining, build a hand-crank or treadle-powered flywheel lathe — with this one tool, you can make every other precision tool.

articles.title: Basic Electricity and Small Generators
articles.body:
Understanding electricity allows salvaging and building power systems from components.

**Basic Electricity Theory**
Voltage (V): electrical pressure. Current (A): flow of electrons. Power (W) = Voltage × Current. Resistance (Ω): opposition to flow.
Ohm's Law: V = I × R (Voltage = Current × Resistance). This one equation describes most DC circuits.

Series circuits: components in a chain. Total resistance adds up. Current is the same throughout.
Parallel circuits: components in branches. Voltage is the same across all branches. Total current is the sum.

**Car Alternator Generator**
A salvaged car alternator can generate significant power. Alternators produce AC, internally rectified to DC. Normal output: 12–14V DC, 40–120 amperes. Requires: external regulator, or the internal regulator can be used.

To use as a wind or water generator: remove the internal regulator (it requires engine-speed RPM to function). Wind the rotor from an external DC source (battery) to create the magnetic field. The rotor must spin at 1,200–1,800 RPM. Use a pulley system to step up the speed from a slower power source.

**Solar Power Basics**
A 100W solar panel in direct sun produces 5–8 ampere-hours per day depending on latitude and season. Connect panels to a charge controller (prevents overcharging) then to a battery bank. 12V lead-acid batteries are most available from salvage.

Series wiring increases voltage. Parallel wiring increases capacity. Fuse every circuit at the positive terminal. Minimum cable sizing: 2.5mm² for 10A, 6mm² for 20A, 10mm² for 30A.

articles.title: Energy Storage — Batteries and Mechanical Systems
articles.body:
Energy storage decouples production from consumption — essential for intermittent sources.

**Lead-Acid Battery Chemistry**
Two lead plates in sulphuric acid electrolyte. During charge: lead sulphate on both plates converts to lead (negative) and lead dioxide (positive). During discharge: reverses.

Care: keep topped up with distilled or deionised water (not tap water). Specific gravity test with hydrometer: 1.28 = fully charged, 1.18 = discharged. Never fully discharge (damages plates). Store partially charged in cool environment.

**Improvised Batteries**
Daniell cell: copper sulphate + zinc sulphate + copper and zinc electrodes. Produces 1.1V. Stack cells in series for useful voltage. Not rechargeable.
Earth battery: zinc and copper rods in moist soil. Produces ~0.5V. Used for telegraph circuits historically. Very low current but continuous.

**Mechanical Energy Storage**
Flywheel: stores rotational kinetic energy. For brief power bursts (machine tools, stamping). A 50kg steel flywheel at 1,000 RPM stores ~2kJ.
Raised water: pump water uphill, release through turbine when energy needed. Energy stored = mass × gravity × height. 1,000 litres raised 10m stores 27Wh. Very scalable with large reservoirs.
Compressed air: pump air into a sealed vessel, release through a motor. Efficiency ~50%. Simple with hand or windmill pump.

domains.label: Materials & Manufacturing
domains.description: Metallurgy, woodworking, ceramics, glass, and textiles. The material foundation of civilisation.

articles.title: Smelting and Iron Production
articles.body:
Iron is the foundation of all industrial technology. Mastering it enables all other manufacturing.

**Ore Identification**
Iron ore: magnetite (black, magnetic), haematite (red-brown), limonite (yellow-brown). Test: a piece of iron ore held near a compass will deflect the needle slightly.

Bog iron: commonly found in swamps and boggy areas as reddish-brown nodules. The most accessible iron ore historically. Renewable — bog iron deposits regenerate in 10–20 years as iron precipitates from groundwater.

**Bloomery Smelting**
The bloomery was humanity's primary iron-making technology for 3,000 years. A clay or stone shaft furnace, 1–1.5m tall, 30–50cm internal diameter.

Procedure: light a fire at the base, add alternating layers of charcoal and crushed iron ore. Blast air with bellows (manual) or tuyere (clay pipe). Maintain temperature above 1,100°C. After 4–6 hours, break open the furnace and retrieve the bloom — a spongy mass of iron and slag.

Bloom processing: reheat to orange-hot. Beat with a heavy hammer to expel slag and consolidate the iron. Repeat many times. This is wrought iron: tough, malleable, relatively soft.

**Carbon Control (Steel)**
Steel is iron with 0.2–2% carbon. More carbon = harder but more brittle. Add carbon by heating iron in charcoal for extended periods (carburisation). Remove carbon by prolonged heating with air exposure (decarburisation). Correct carbon level by look: high carbon steel forms a very fine grain structure when broken.

**Heat Treatment**
Hardening: heat to non-magnetic temperature (check with magnet), quench in water or oil. Water quench = harder but more brittle. Oil = slightly softer but tougher.
Tempering: reheat hardened steel to 200–300°C (observe colour: pale yellow = 220°C, blue = 300°C). Cool in air. Reduces brittleness while retaining most hardness.

articles.title: Blacksmithing and Bronze Working
articles.body:
Basic smithing allows making and repairing every essential tool.

**Blacksmithing Fundamentals**
Forge: a firepot containing fuel (charcoal or coke), air blast from bellows or electric fan. Work metal at bright orange to yellow-white heat (1,000–1,300°C). Metal at red heat is too cold to work efficiently and may crack.

Basic operations:
Drawing out: hammer on the face of the anvil with glancing blows to lengthen and thin metal.
Upsetting: push metal into itself to thicken it. Strike end-on.
Punching: drive a punch through hot metal to create a hole.
Drifting: enlarge a hole with a tapered tool.
Bending: over the horn of the anvil or around a mandrel.

**Essential Tools You Can Make**
A hammer, tongs, chisel, punch, and hardy (a chisel set in the anvil's hardy hole) are the minimum set. All can be made from iron bar with a forge, anvil, and hammer. Anvil: a mass of dense iron or steel. A railway track section works. A large stone works for light work.

**Bronze (Copper-Tin Alloy)**
Bronze is 90% copper, 10% tin. Melts at 950°C (much lower than iron's 1,538°C). Can be smelted in a simple pottery kiln.
Malachite (green copper ore) and cassiterite (tin ore, black, heavy) are the raw materials. Smelt each separately, alloy together in liquid form. Cast into open moulds of stone or clay, or lost-wax casting for complex shapes.

Copper alone (smelted from malachite at 1,085°C) is useful for wire, roofing, and vessels. Bronze is harder and more durable for tools.

articles.title: Ceramics and Glass Production
articles.body:
Ceramics are essential for food storage, cooking, and laboratory equipment. Glass enables optics.

**Ceramics**
Clay identification: plastic clay moults smoothly without cracking. Test by rolling a thin coil and bending — if it doesn't crack, it's suitable.

Primary methods:
Coiling: roll clay into ropes, stack in circles, blend joins. Pinching: press and pull a ball of clay between thumb and fingers. Slab building: roll clay flat, cut and join slabs with slurry (liquid clay).

Drying: dry slowly (weeks) in shade to avoid cracking. Fast drying causes uneven shrinkage and cracks.

Firing: pit firing — pack pots in a pit with fuel, burn fast and hot, unearth after cooling. Achieves 600–900°C. Sufficient for functional pottery. Kiln firing: build a kiln from bricks or clay, fuel from below, achieve 1,000–1,300°C for stronger, waterproof stoneware.

**Glass Production**
Basic glass: silica (sand) 72%, soda ash (sodium carbonate) 15%, lime (calcium oxide) 13%. Melt at 1,400–1,500°C in a crucible (ceramic container) in a hot kiln.

Soda ash from wood ash: dissolve wood ash in water, boil down to concentrate, the residue contains potassium carbonate (potash) and sodium carbonate. Historically called potash. It lowers the melting point of silica.

Glass blowing: gather molten glass on a blowpipe, blow while rotating to form vessels. Window glass (crown method): blow a sphere, cut off ends, reheat and spin to open into a disc.

**Optical Lenses**
A convex (magnifying) lens can be ground from glass by progressively polishing with abrasive compounds (sand, then finer abrasive, then polishing compound) against a concave mould. A lens provides: reading aid, fire starting, telescope/microscope construction. Telescope enables navigation, astronomy, and long-range observation.

articles.title: Carpentry Tools and Joinery
articles.body:
Wood is the most versatile building and manufacturing material in temperate zones.

**Essential Hand Tools**
Axe: tree felling, rough shaping. Adze: hollowing, smoothing flat surfaces. Hand saw: crosscutting and ripping. Drawknife: shaping green wood quickly. Chisel: joinery, carving. Plane: smoothing flat surfaces. Brace and bit: drilling holes.

All can be made with basic blacksmithing. A complete set of hand tools requires less than 10kg of iron.

**Green vs. Dry Wood**
Green (freshly cut) wood is easy to shape but will crack as it dries. Dry wood is dimensionally stable but hard to cut. Strategy: rough-shape green, allow to dry partially, final-cut, allow to finish drying.

**Wood Selection by Use**
Structural beams: oak, ash, Douglas fir (strong and stiff).
Handles and tool handles: ash, hickory (springy, absorbs shock).
Furniture: oak, walnut, cherry (stable, finishes well).
Bowls and kitchen items: cherry, maple, sycamore (food-safe).
Steam bending: ash, oak, elm (flexible when steamed, hold shape when dried).
Arrow shafts: straight-grained cedar, birch, or any light straight wood.

**Joinery for Structural Work**
Mortise-and-tenon: the foundation of timber frame construction. The tenon (protruding tongue) fits tightly into the mortise (slot). Wedge or peg to lock. No glue or hardware required.

Dovetail: angled interlocking pins and tails. Extremely strong against tension. Used in drawer corners, box construction. Cannot pull apart.

Scarfjoint: joins two pieces end-to-end, lengthening them. Must be in a low-stress location or reinforced.

articles.title: Fibre, Spinning, and Weaving
articles.body:
Textiles protect against cold and provide trade goods.

**Plant Fibres**
Flax (linen): strongest plant fibre. Process: ret (soak stems in water 2 weeks), dry, break, scutch (beat to remove woody parts), hackle (comb to align fibres). Spin into yarn.
Nettle: similar to flax. Process the same way. Strong durable fibre historically used across Europe.
Cotton: in warm climates. Seed cotton → gin (remove seeds) → card (fluff and align) → spin.
Hemp: strong, coarse fibre. Similar to flax processing. Excellent rope and canvas.

**Spinning**
Drop spindle: the simplest spinning tool. A weighted disc on a stick. Draft (pull out and thin) fibres with one hand while the spindle spins on the other end, twisting fibres into yarn. Practice needed but learnable in hours.

Spinning wheel: dramatically faster than drop spindle. Build from wood — requires a flywheel, spindle, and treadle mechanism. Wheel diameter 60cm drives spindle at 10:1 ratio.

**Weaving**
Backstrap loom: stretched between a tree and the weaver's body. Most portable loom. Used across the developing world. Produces fabric of any width up to ~60cm.
Rigid heddle loom: simple frame loom with a rigid heddle (combined heddle and beater). Faster than backstrap. Good for beginners.
Floor loom: multiple harnesses allow complex patterns. Fastest production. Build from timber.

**Natural Dyes**
Weld (yellow), woad/indigo (blue), madder (red), walnut shells (brown/black), onion skins (orange/yellow). Mordant the cloth first (alum, iron, tannin) to fix the dye. Boil cloth in mordant, wring, boil in dye bath.

domains.label: Communication Systems
domains.description: Information storage, transmission, and preservation. From signal fires to radio networks.

articles.title: Signal Systems and Information Storage
articles.body:
